milestones.title: the verifier, sampling and KL
milestones.task: Write parse_number(text) (a Fraction, or None when the text is not a number), reward(text, answer) (1.0 or 0.0), sample_index(probs, rng) and kl_divergence(p, q).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks eight surface forms that must parse to the right value (including "0.1" as an exact tenth), nine strings that must give None, ten rewards, that the task's verifier finds 2, 1, 2, 1, ... correct candidates per question, six scripted draws that must pick the right index with exactly one rng.random() call each, that a zero-probability index is never drawn, the frequencies of 20,000 seeded draws, and a hand-computed KL, its asymmetry and its non-negativity.
milestones.explain:
A verifiable reward (chapter 14) is computed by a program that checks the answer against ground truth. Here the program reads an answer string and returns 1.0 if it is the true number and 0.0 otherwise. Three details decide whether the verifier can be trusted, because the policy will search for every loophole you leave.

  • Exact, not approximate. fractions.Fraction("0.1") is exactly one tenth; float("0.1") is not, and comparing floats invites a tolerance that someone will tune until a wrong answer passes. With Fraction, "3.91e2" and "782/2" are exactly 391 and "391.0000001" is not.
  • Junk is a zero, not an error. Fraction("about 391") raises ValueError. A verifier that crashes on a hedge stops the training run; one that returns 0.0 trains the policy away from hedging. Chapter 14's lazy verifier, which gave credit for any answer that mentioned 391, rewarded exactly the hedges in this task.
  • Normalise the surface, not the meaning. Leading and trailing whitespace and leading zeros are surface; whether the answer is right is meaning.

Sampling should be exactly reproducible, so the lab fixes the method. sample_index(probs, rng) makes one call to rng.random(), call it u, and returns the first index whose running total of probabilities exceeds u. That is inverse-CDF sampling, and the strict inequality matters: an index with probability zero must never be drawn, even when u = 0.0. Fixing the recipe also means the checker can regenerate your preference pairs in milestone 3 and compare them exactly.

Finally the leash. The exact KL divergence KL(p ‖ q) = ∑k pk log(pk / qk) measures how far a policy p has moved from a reference q (entropy, cross-entropy and KL). It is zero only when they are equal, never negative, and not symmetric. With a tabular policy you can compute it exactly, which will let you check chapter 14's sample-based estimator in milestone 5.

milestones.title: the DPO loss and its gradient
milestones.task: Write implicit_rewards(zq, zref_q, beta) (the list of β (log πθ − log πref) for the six candidates of one question), dpo_margin(zq, zref_q, w, l, beta), dpo_loss(z, ref, pairs, beta) (mean over pairs (q, w, l)) and dpo_grads(z, ref, pairs, beta) (a gradient shaped like z, also averaged over pairs). Use the given log_softmax and sigmoid.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand values (implicit rewards 2 ln 1.5 and 2 ln 0.5 for a 0.75/0.25 policy against a uniform reference, margin 2 ln 3, loss ln(1 + 1/9)), that the implicit reward is zero at the reference and unchanged when a constant is added to every logit, a hand-computed gradient [−0.25, 0, 0.25] and that two identical pairs give the same gradient as one, a finite-difference check of every logit gradient on seeded random problems, and the extremes: a margin of +40 gives a weight of essentially 0, a margin of −1600 gives a finite loss near 1600 and a gradient of −β.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 12 derived the DPO loss from the KL-regularised objective in five moves. Take a prompt x, a chosen answer yw and a rejected answer yl. The implicit reward of an answer is how much the policy has raised its log-probability above the reference's, scaled by β:

r̂(y) = β · [ log πθ(y | x) − log πref(y | x) ]

The margin of a pair is m = r̂(yw) − r̂(yl), and the loss is −log σ(m), the Bradley-Terry log-likelihood of the observed choice with the policy as its own reward model. The dataset loss is the mean over pairs. Three consequences are worth seeing in code before any training.

  • The starting loss is exactly ln 2. At πθ = πref every implicit reward is zero, the margin is zero and −log σ(0) = log 2 = 0.693. A DPO run that does not start there has a bug, usually in which model the reference is.
  • The gradient is tiny. Write the log-probability of candidate k as zk − logsumexp(z). In the margin, the two logsumexp terms are the same number (it is the same question's softmax) and they cancel, so m = β [ (zw − zl) − (zrefw − zrefl) ]. The margin depends on the logits of exactly two candidates. With ∂(−log σ(m))/∂m = −σ(−m), the gradient of one pair is ∂L/∂zw = −β σ(−m), ∂L/∂zl = +β σ(−m) and zero on every other logit. This is chapter 12's gradient, −β σ(−m) [∇ log π(yw) − ∇ log π(yl)], specialised to a softmax: the −p terms in ∇ log π = e − p are the same for both answers and cancel in the bracket.
  • The weight is self-limiting. σ(−m) is near 1 when the pair is ranked the wrong way and near 0 when it is ranked right by a wide margin. A pair stops pulling once the policy has learned it. The script below trains on 400 pairs with β = 0.5 and reports the mean weight over the pairs as it falls.
$ python3 exp_dpo_weights.py
400 pairs from the reference policy, beta = 0.5
 step    loss  mean margin  pairs ranked right  mean weight sigmoid(-m)
    0   0.693        0.000                0.00                    0.500
   10   0.415        0.691                1.00                    0.337
   30   0.229        1.463                1.00                    0.200
  100   0.090        2.603                1.00                    0.084
  300   0.033        3.737                1.00                    0.032

The loss falls from 0.693 to 0.033 and the mean weight from 0.500 to 0.032 over 300 steps: by the end almost every pair is ranked correctly by a wide margin (mean margin 3.7) and hardly pulls at all. The same trace at β = 0.1, the TRL default, would be far slower, because β multiplies the margin: the same logit change produces one fifth the margin.

milestones.title: preference pairs and DPO training
milestones.task: Write make_pairs(task, n, rng, max_attempts=None) following the procedure above exactly (the order of random draws matters, see the docstring) and train_dpo(task, pairs, beta, lr, steps), which copies task.ref, records the loss before each step, and descends. It returns (z, losses).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It compares your pairs, for two seeds, with an independent implementation of the procedure; checks that every chosen answer is verified correct and every rejected one wrong, that max_attempts caps the draws, and that task.ref is not modified. For training it checks that the first loss is ln 2, that gradient descent with a small learning rate never goes uphill, that a question with no pairs keeps its reference logits exactly, that 400 pairs lift the expected reward by at least 0.35 and the greedy accuracy to at least 0.67, that after training every correct answer's implicit reward exceeds every wrong one's on the four easiest questions, and that fewer steps mean less drift.
milestones.explain:
DPO needs a dataset of comparisons. In chapter 12 these come from people; for a task with a verifier you can build them mechanically, which is how most open recipes produce DPO data for maths and code. The procedure the lab fixes is: pick a question at random, draw two answers from the reference policy, ask the verifier for both rewards, and keep the pair only if the rewards differ, with the higher-reward answer as yw. Pairs where both answers are right or both are wrong carry no preference and are thrown away.

That rejection step has a cost that deserves a number. A question on which the reference is right with probability p yields a usable pair with probability 2p(1 − p): 0.48 at p = 0.6, but 0.03 at p = 0.015 and 0.016 at p = 0.008. The hardest questions rarely produce a pair at all. Getting 400 pairs from the reference takes 3,074 sampled answers in this task, and the pairs are not spread evenly over the questions: question 0 contributes 67 pairs, question 7 contributes 15 and question 11 contributes 1.

Training is then plain full-batch gradient descent on the logits, starting from the reference: the logits are the parameters, and the gradient is the one you wrote in milestone 2. After it, the policy is its own reward model. The script shows what the implicit reward looks like on two questions after 300 steps at β = 0.1:

$ python3 exp_implicit.py
question 961 - 418 = 543   (66 training pairs)
     candidate  verifier  pi_ref  pi_dpo  implicit reward
           534         0   0.112   0.000           -0.927
           543         1   0.450   1.000            0.080
           553         0   0.117   0.000           -1.101
           443         0   0.112   0.000           -0.954
          1379         0   0.087   0.000           -0.954
    543 or 544         0   0.122   0.000           -0.966
question 36 x 16 = 576   (27 training pairs)
     candidate  verifier  pi_ref  pi_dpo  implicit reward
           566         0   0.379   0.003           -0.482
           576         1   0.160   0.974            0.181
           575         0   0.072   0.005           -0.265
            52         0   0.106   0.005           -0.298
           586         0   0.126   0.005           -0.314
    576 or 577         0   0.157   0.007           -0.314

On question 1 the correct answer's implicit reward is positive (+0.080) and all five wrong answers are around −1.0, so the policy ranks them as the verifier does, and it puts probability 1.000 on the right answer. Look at question 5 too: the reference preferred the wrong answer 566 (0.379 against 0.160 for the right one), and the implicit reward of 566 is the most negative among the wrong ones (−0.482) because it fell the furthest. Chapter 12's warning applies here as well: DPO only constrains the difference of implicit rewards, and on a chosen answer that already has high reference probability, the implicit reward can be small even though the probability is near 1.

milestones.title: group-relative advantages
milestones.task: Write group_advantages(rewards, mode="std", eps=1e-4), returning one advantage per reward for the three modes, and zero_signal(rewards), true when every reward in the group is the same. A tied group must give exact zeros in every mode, with no division by zero.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the chapter's numbers for one correct answer in eight in all three modes, two-of-four giving ±1, exact zeros for all-wrong and all-correct groups in every mode, zero_signal on five cases, and on seeded random groups that the standardised and mean-only advantages sum to zero, that leave-one-out equals G / (G − 1) times mean-only, and that standardised advantages do not change when the rewards are rescaled and shifted. It then enumerates every group for G = 2, 3 and 4 and checks that the expected gradient is (G − 1)/G of the true gradient for "mean" and exactly 1 for "rloo".
milestones.explain:
GRPO throws away the pairs and the reward model's replacement, the implicit reward, and starts from a different question: given a handful of answers to the same question, which ones were better than the rest? For each question it samples a group of G answers from the current policy and scores each with the verifier to get rewards r1, …, rG. The advantage of answer i is its reward standardised within the group (equation 3 of the DeepSeek-R1 paper, as chapter 14 writes it):

Ai = ( ri − mean(r) ) / ( std(r) + ε )

The lab uses the population standard deviation (divide by G) and a small ε = 10-4 so that a tied group divides by something non-zero. Two simpler rules appear in the literature and in libraries, and you implement all three behind a mode argument:

  • "std" as above: GRPO as published.
  • "mean": ri − mean(r), without the division (the choice Liu et al., 2025, argue for in "Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training", the variant sometimes called Dr. GRPO).
  • "rloo": ri − the mean of the other G − 1 rewards, the leave-one-out baseline of RLOO (Ahmadian et al., 2024).

The numbers are worth looking at once. For a group of eight and every possible count of correct answers:

$ python3 exp_advantages.py
correct | std: right   wrong  sum|A| | mean: right   wrong | rloo: right   wrong
      0 |          -   0.000    0.00 |           -   0.000 |           -   0.000
      1 |      2.645  -0.378    5.29 |       0.875  -0.125 |       1.000  -0.143
      2 |      1.732  -0.577    6.93 |       0.750  -0.250 |       0.857  -0.286
      3 |      1.291  -0.774    7.74 |       0.625  -0.375 |       0.714  -0.429
      4 |      1.000  -1.000    8.00 |       0.500  -0.500 |       0.571  -0.571
      5 |      0.774  -1.291    7.74 |       0.375  -0.625 |       0.429  -0.714
      6 |      0.577  -1.732    6.93 |       0.250  -0.750 |       0.286  -0.857
      7 |      0.378  -2.645    5.29 |       0.125  -0.875 |       0.143  -1.000
      8 |      0.000       -    0.00 |       0.000       - |       0.000       -

Read the first row of numbers. With one correct answer in eight, the standardised rule gives the winner +2.645 and each loser −0.378, a total pull of 5.29; the mean-only rule gives +0.875 and −0.125. The standard deviation boosts the rare event: a prompt where the model almost always fails or almost always succeeds is weighted up compared with a 50-50 prompt, which is a choice, not a fact, and the reason the two rules differ in practice. The leave-one-out advantage is always G / (G − 1) = 8/7 times the mean-only advantage. The top and bottom rows are all zeros: a group where every answer ties has no signal, whichever rule you use.

Is the group mean a valid baseline?

Chapter 7 proved that subtracting a baseline b leaves the policy gradient unbiased if b does not depend on the action being scored. The group mean contains ri itself, so it is not independent of answer i, and chapter 14 computed the consequence: the expected gradient is (G − 1)/G of the true one. In a tabular policy you can check this exactly, with no sampling at all, by enumerating every possible group of G answers, weighting each by its probability and summing the gradient estimator (1/G) ∑ Ai ∇ log π(oi):

$ python3 exp_bias.py
true gradient on the correct answer's logit: 0.2237
G = 2: expected gradient / true gradient: mean baseline 0.500 (theory 0.500), leave-one-out 1.000
G = 3: expected gradient / true gradient: mean baseline 0.667 (theory 0.667), leave-one-out 1.000
G = 4: expected gradient / true gradient: mean baseline 0.750 (theory 0.750), leave-one-out 1.000
G = 5: expected gradient / true gradient: mean baseline 0.800 (theory 0.800), leave-one-out 1.000

With the group mean as the baseline the expected gradient is exactly 0.500, 0.667, 0.750 and 0.800 of the true one for G = 2 to 5; with the leave-one-out baseline it is exactly 1.000. The direction is right, the size is too small by 1/G, and in practice a constant factor on the gradient is absorbed by the learning rate, which is why GRPO works anyway. The test in check.py repeats this enumeration on your group_advantages.

milestones.title: the GRPO objective for one group
milestones.task: Write ratio(zq, zold_q, a), clipped_objective(rho, adv, eps) (the quantity to maximise for one sample), k3(zq, zref_q, a) and grpo_loss_and_grad(zq, zold_q, zref_q, actions, advs, eps, beta), which returns (loss, dz) for one group: the mean loss above and its gradient with respect to the six logits zq.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks ratios of 1.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (and invariance to adding a constant to the logits), nine values of the clipped term including both sides of the clip, two hand values of k3 (0.19315 and 0.30685) and non-negativity; at the reference it checks the loss (0) and the REINFORCE gradient [−0.5, 0.5, 0]; it checks that a clipped sample has an exactly zero gradient and an unclipped sample on the other side of the range does not; that the KL term alone has gradient (1 − πref/πθ)(ea − p); and on seeded random groups, with some samples clipped, that the loss is the formula above and every component of dz agrees with a finite difference.
milestones.explain:
With advantages in hand, GRPO uses PPO's machinery from chapter 8. Freeze a copy of the policy as πold and sample the group from it. The probability ratio of a sampled answer a is ρ = πθ(a) / πold(a), which is exactly 1 on the first gradient step and drifts away as the policy changes. Each sample contributes the clipped surrogate min(ρ A, clip(ρ, 1 − ε, 1 + ε) A), to be maximised, and a KL penalty to the reference. Written as a loss to minimise, averaged over the group (a one-token answer has no inner sum over tokens):

L = −(1/G) ∑i min( ρi Ai, clip(ρi, 1−ε, 1+ε) Ai )  +  β (1/G) ∑i k3i

The penalty uses the k3 estimator of chapter 8, computed from the one sampled answer: with r = πref(a) / πθ(a), k3 = r − log r − 1. It is never negative, it is zero when the two policies agree on a, and its expectation under samples from πθ is the exact KL, which is what the sampled penalty is estimating. You can compare the two on the trained policies below.

The plot shows why the clip is a one-sided safety rail. For a good answer (A > 0), the objective grows with ρ until ρ = 1 + ε and is flat after: the policy has already raised this answer's probability by 20%, and the objective offers nothing for more. For a bad answer (A < 0) it mirrors that below 1 − ε. On the other side nothing is clipped, because the min picks the more pessimistic of the two terms: a good answer whose probability has fallen (ρ < 1 − ε) still has the full gradient to push it back up.

The gradient, by hand

For a softmax, ∂ log π(a) / ∂z = ea − p (the one-hot vector of the sampled answer minus the probabilities), so ∂ρ/∂z = ρ (ea − p). A sample's policy term has gradient −ρ A (ea − p) while the clip is inactive, and exactly zero while it is active: when A > 0 and ρ > 1 + ε, or A < 0 and ρ < 1 − ε. For the KL term, ∂k3/∂ log π = 1 − r, so its gradient is (1 − πref(a) / πθ(a)) (ea − p), which pulls an answer the policy has made likelier than the reference back down, and an answer it has made less likely back up. At πθ = πold = πref the whole thing collapses to the plain advantage-weighted REINFORCE gradient of chapter 7, −(1/G) ∑ Ai (eai − p), which is also the hand case in the check.

The clip's effect is easiest to see by taking many gradient steps on a single group, which is what a training loop that reuses a batch does. The script samples one group of eight answers for question 3, then repeats the update with and without the clip:

$ python3 exp_clip.py
question 233 + 242: group rewards [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1], advantages [-0.58, -0.58, -0.58, -0.58, -0.58, -0.58, 1.73, 1.73]

eps = 0.2   lr 1.0, beta 0
 step  max rho (A>0)  min rho (A<0)  clipped samples  P(correct)
    0          1.000          1.000                0       0.280
    1          1.421          0.742                7       0.398
    2          1.448          0.745                7       0.406
    3          1.475          0.748                8       0.413
    4          1.475          0.748                8       0.413
    5          1.475          0.748                8       0.413
    6          1.475          0.748                8       0.413
    7          1.475          0.748                8       0.413
    8          1.475          0.748                8       0.413

no clip (eps = 100)   lr 1.0, beta 0
 step  max rho (A>0)  min rho (A<0)  clipped samples  P(correct)
    0          1.000          1.000                0       0.280
    1          1.421          0.742                0       0.398
    2          1.961          0.505                0       0.549
    3          2.479          0.322                0       0.694
    4          2.835          0.209                0       0.794
    5          3.044          0.146                0       0.852
    6          3.169          0.110                0       0.887
    7          3.249          0.087                0       0.910
    8          3.304          0.072                0       0.925

The group has two correct answers (advantage +1.73) and six wrong ones (−0.58). With ε = 0.2, one step at learning rate 1.0 already moves the ratio of the best sample to 1.42, beyond the clip range, and from then on seven or eight of the eight samples are clipped and the gradient is zero: the probability of a correct answer stops at 0.413. Without a clip the same updates continue (ratios of 3.3 and 0.07) and the probability of a correct answer climbs to 0.925 on the strength of eight samples. That is the point of the trust region: eight samples are a noisy estimate of which answers are good, and the clip stops the policy moving far on the strength of them.

milestones.title: the GRPO training loop and the comparison
milestones.task: Write train_grpo(task, steps, group_size=8, batch_questions=6, inner=4, lr=0.5, eps=0.2, beta=0.04, mode="std", seed=0). It returns (z, log): the trained logits (starting from a copy of task.ref) and one dict per step, {"reward": expected reward after the step, "zero_groups": number of silent groups in that step}. The docstring fixes the order of random draws and the inner loop.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks that task.ref is not modified, that the log has one correct entry per step and the same seed gives the same run, that 60 steps lift the expected reward above 0.70 and the greedy accuracy to at least 0.75, that between 100 and 300 of the 360 groups are silent and that more are silent in the last ten steps than in the first ten, that questions 10 and 11 are not solved by accident, that β = 1.0 holds the KL below 60% of the unpenalised run and costs reward, that reusing each batch four times learns faster than once, and that the mean-only and leave-one-out modes also learn. It also trains DPO and checks that it, too, leaves question 10 and 11 unsolved.
milestones.explain:
Now the loop that chapter 14 draws as a stepper. Each iteration of train_grpo picks six of the twelve questions, and for each one: freezes πold, samples a group of eight answers from it, scores them with the verifier, standardises the rewards into advantages, then takes inner = 4 gradient steps on the same group (with πold held fixed, so the ratios drift and the clip can act). Reusing a batch is what the clip is for: generating the group is the expensive part of a real run, and the clip makes it safe to extract several steps from it. Sixty iterations, six groups each, is 2,880 sampled answers.

Here is how the two methods compare after training, on the same twelve questions. DPO uses the 400 pairs from milestone 3 and the GRPO run is the default. The right-hand columns show two DPO runs because 300 steps leaves it still climbing:

$ python3 exp_compare.py
 q   question       ref   DPO 300  DPO 1000   GRPO 60
 0  317 + 335     0.600     1.000     1.000     0.977
 1  961 - 418     0.450     1.000     1.000     0.972
 2    28 x 20     0.350     1.000     1.000     0.957
 3  233 + 242     0.280     1.000     1.000     0.976
 4  908 - 390     0.220     0.995     1.000     0.963
 5    36 x 16     0.160     0.974     1.000     0.961
 6  458 + 448     0.120     0.913     1.000     0.963
 7  631 - 161     0.080     0.653     0.998     0.957
 8    13 x 31     0.050     0.349     0.982     0.968
 9  343 + 212     0.030     0.087     0.495     0.933
10  629 - 456     0.015     0.049     0.310     0.030
11    32 x 23     0.008     0.010     0.017     0.008
             --------- --------- --------- ---------
         mean    0.197     0.669     0.817     0.806
    KL to ref     0.00      0.92      1.51      1.43

samples drawn from the reference to build the 400 pairs: 3,074; GRPO samples: 2,880

Four things to read from this.

  • Both methods work. The expected reward rises from 0.197 to 0.806 (GRPO, 60 steps) and 0.817 (DPO, 1,000 steps), with almost identical drift from the reference (KL 1.43 and 1.51). At 300 steps DPO has only reached 0.669; its gradient is scaled by β = 0.1, so it needs more steps for the same movement. The comparison is not a verdict on which algorithm is better, only a demonstration that in a tabular toy both fit the same verifier. The real differences (DPO needs no sampling during training; GRPO uses the policy's own samples; their memory cost is chapter 12's and 14's tables) live outside this toy.
  • They need similar amounts of generation. The 400 pairs cost 3,074 sampled answers from the reference, because most pairs tie and are discarded; GRPO drew 2,880. Offline data is not free data.
  • The hard questions behave differently. On question 9 (reference 3% right) GRPO reaches 0.933 and DPO 0.495. On question 10 (reference 1.5%) DPO reaches 0.310 and GRPO stays at 0.030. DPO's pairs are a filtered dataset: of 3,074 samples, only the lucky ones that contain a correct answer next to a wrong one survive, and DPO then trains on all of them hard. GRPO's groups of eight on question 10 are all wrong about 89% of the time at the reference (and 78% at the end), and those groups do nothing.
  • Neither can learn question 11. With 0.8% reference success, a pair or a group with a correct answer is a rare accident: one pair in 400, and only about 6% of groups of eight at the reference contain a correct answer. Both methods inherit the same ceiling: RL with a verifier can only sharpen what the reference sometimes does, a point chapter 14 returns to when it discusses what RLVR adds to a model.

The leash is the other thing to study. The script sweeps β for both methods:

$ python3 exp_beta.py
reference: expected reward 0.197

        method   beta  expected reward  greedy acc  KL to ref
           DPO   0.05            0.570        0.67      0.607
           DPO   0.10            0.669        0.75      0.921
           DPO   0.50            0.788        0.83      1.298
           DPO   1.00            0.744        0.83      1.070
          GRPO   0.00            0.811        0.83      1.470
          GRPO   0.04            0.806        0.83      1.427
          GRPO   0.20            0.772        0.83      1.234
          GRPO   1.00            0.536        0.83      0.438

In DPO, β is the dial of the closed-form optimum π* ∝ πref exp(r/β): at 1.0 the reward and the drift are both lower than at 0.5 for the same number of steps. In GRPO a coefficient of 1.0 holds the policy to KL 0.44 and an expected reward of 0.536, against 1.47 and 0.811 with no penalty; 0.04 is almost the same as none. The same β has different effects in different methods, because DPO's multiplies the margin inside a sigmoid and GRPO's multiplies a penalty added to the loss. Libraries' defaults differ for the same reason: TRL's GRPO default is 0.0, DPO's is 0.1.

Finally, the groups that teach nothing. The script counts them over a 60-step run and, for each question, compares the reference's chance of an all-wrong group with the trained policy's chance of an all-right one:

$ python3 exp_zero_signal.py
194 of 360 groups had zero signal over 60 steps (6 questions x 60 steps)
first 10 steps: 18 of 60;   last 10 steps: 39 of 60

 1  961 - 418  0.450   0.972                0.008                0.799
